title: Лёва в роли Шефа  (Lyova Playing the Role of the Chef)

segments.t: While Sasha tells Max that she could not stay with her aunt, the VIP guest's assistant slips past the dining room and heads straight into the kitchen demanding to see the chef. Thinking fast, the crew shoves Lyova into the office so he can pretend to be Viktor Petrovich.
Там какая-то девушка сюда идет, хочет видеть шефа.
Где я могу найти вашего шеф-повара?
Я же просил меня не беспокоить.
Alright, let's go through it step by step in English.
'Did it not work out staying at your aunt's place?' In Russian, the idea of 'not' flows naturally into 'to stop' without extra filler words.
'Yes, her father-in-law is coming to visit her.' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'yes' before landing on 'is arriving'.
'So it did not work out.' In Russian, the idea of 'not' flows naturally into 'worked out' without extra filler words. Kostya answers right away.
'All right then.' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'come on' and finishing on 'really?!'.
'Well, it is no big deal.' Chef Viktor brings out the contrast between 'come on' and 'nothing' in a few short words.
'Maybe.' The meaning hinges on 'maybe' working together with 'maybe' in spoken Russian. Chef Viktor answers right away.
Там какая-то девушка сюда идет, хочет видеть шефа.
'Some woman is walking this way, she wants to see the Chef.' Notice how Russian expresses 'there' and 'chef' with crisp inflection rather than helper words.
'We stick to the plan.' Kostya anchors the line on 'we work', while 'plan' completes the thought.
Где я могу найти вашего шеф-повара?
'Where can I find your head chef?' Chef Viktor raises the pitch on 'head chef' to turn the phrase into a direct spoken question. Kostya answers right away.
'In his office, of course.' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'office' before landing on 'of course'.
Я же просил меня не беспокоить.
'I specifically asked not to be disturbed.' The grammar packs 'I' and 'to bother' into a tight, idiomatic kitchen exchange.
'I am preparing the new menu.' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'I' and finishing on 'menu'. Chef Viktor answers right away.
'Close that damn door!' In Russian, the idea of 'close' flows naturally into 'the door' without extra filler words. Alright, let's listen to all those lines again from the top.
Там какая-то девушка сюда идет, хочет видеть шефа.
Где я могу найти вашего шеф-повара?
Я же просил меня не беспокоить.
